\vspace*{-4em}
\begin{abstract}
Hawaii's March 2020 mandatory traveler quarantine sealed the state's borders at the same instant the COVID-19 pandemic collapsed global travel demand. For a single treated unit these two forces are perfectly collinear in time, so the conventional synthetic-control toolkit---which matches the treated series to a counterfactual that is itself battered by the pandemic---cannot separate the border-closure \emph{policy} from the coincident \emph{pandemic}. I address this with Single Proxy Synthetic Control (SPSC), a member of the proximal / negative-control family that does not attempt to remove the latent pandemic factor but instead \emph{instruments} it using insulated employment sectors that carry the pandemic's macro-recession shock yet are immune to the border policy. Contrasting SPSC against a naive Synthetic Historical Control baseline shows that a substantial share of the measured tourism collapse is pandemic contamination the naive design cannot net out. SPSC recovers a large, robust tourism-demand collapse (roughly 60--75 percentage points of year-over-year growth for the visitor-volume series) but, because the insulated sectors span only the macro-recession factor and not the travel-demand-collapse factor, identifies it only weakly-to-borderline (pre-period RMSE/SD $\approx 0.9$--$1.0$); these tourism effects are therefore best read as \emph{upper bounds in magnitude} on the policy effect and are reported as a robustness band. The one cleanly identified series is the broad Coincident Economic Activity Index (RMSE/SD $0.67$, a $\sim$12 point drop). The paper demonstrates how negative-control inference disciplines causal claims when a policy and a global shock arrive together.
\keywords{Proximal Causal Inference, Negative Controls, Synthetic Control, Policy Evaluation, COVID-19}
\end{abstract}

# Introduction

Among all U.S. states, Hawaii implemented perhaps the most extreme and comprehensive economic shutdown in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper studies the short-run economic consequences of Hawaii's March 2020 mandatory quarantine \citep[]{Yan01022022}. Unlike most regions that experienced economic contraction from COVID-19 through voluntary distancing, fear, or uneven mandates, Hawaii implemented one of the few deliberate and coordinated state-level shutdowns in the United States. This policy was aimed not merely at mitigating the virus, but at suppressing travel and commerce altogether. On March 26, 2020, the state imposed a mandatory 14-day quarantine on all arrivals, effectively sealing its borders.

This paper addresses a core policy question: What are the economic costs of decisive early action in the face of an uncertain crisis? While much has been written about the epidemiological and social effects of COVID-19 interventions, less is known about their economic toll. This is especially true in cases where policymakers opted for maximal containment. The most famous case was Wuhan's January 2020 lockdown, as studied by \cite{hubeipda}. However, work outside of this context is rare. Understanding these costs is essential not just for pandemic preparedness, but for future crises, such as climate shocks or geopolitical disruptions, where early intervention may again carry significant short-run economic risks in exchange for long-term societal benefits \citep[]{newman2023global}.

Estimating that cost, however, runs into an identification problem that is easy to overlook and fatal if ignored. Hawaii closed its border at the same instant the pandemic collapsed global travel demand. For a single treated unit these two forces---the *policy* and the *pandemic*---are perfectly collinear in time: every post-March-2020 month is simultaneously a "quarantine" month and a "pandemic" month. This is a coincident common shock, and it breaks the standard causal toolkit. A classical synthetic control or difference-in-differences design matches Hawaii to a counterfactual and reads a good pre-treatment fit as evidence of credibility. But any counterfactual Hawaii---whether built from other states or from Hawaii's own history---is a "no-quarantine" world that is *also* a "no-pandemic" world, because the design has no way to hold the pandemic fixed while switching the policy off. The resulting estimate is the border-closure effect **plus** whatever pandemic-driven demand loss Hawaii would have suffered anyway, and pre-fit quality says nothing about the size of that contamination.

The contribution of this paper is to take that identification problem seriously and to resolve it with the right tool. The confounder here---the pandemic---is a time-varying latent factor that moves the outcome and coincides with treatment timing; it cannot be conditioned away (it is unobserved) and it cannot be matched away (it moves any donor too). The *proximal* answer \citep{miao2018identifying,tchetgen2024introduction} is not to remove the confounder but to **instrument** it: find observable "negative controls" that are driven by the same latent pandemic factor but carry **no causal path from the treatment**, and use them to algebraically subtract the pandemic out of the counterfactual. In this setting the negative controls are **insulated employment sectors**---industries hit by the pandemic recession but not downstream of whether tourists can physically arrive in Hawaii. I implement this through **Single Proxy Synthetic Control (SPSC)** \citep{parktchetgen2025}, the member of the proximal family suited to a single treated unit with a single proxy group.

Empirically, contrasting SPSC against a naive Synthetic Historical Control (SHC) baseline \citep{SHC} makes the identification point concrete: the gap between the two estimates is the pandemic's macro-recession component that the naive design silently loads onto the policy. SPSC recovers a large and robust tourism-demand collapse, but I am careful about what it identifies. Because the insulated sectors span the pandemic's general-recession factor and not its travel-demand-collapse factor, the SPSC tourism estimates over-attribute the drop to the policy and are best read as *upper bounds in magnitude* on the border-closure effect. I therefore report them as a robustness band rather than as point estimates, discipline each effect with a relevance diagnostic, and single out the one cleanly identified outcome---the broad Economic Activity Index---as the most trustworthy number.

The remainder of the paper proceeds as follows. Section \ref{sec:bgresearch} reviews prior research on early pandemic interventions and the methodological challenge of studying one-off, jurisdiction-wide policies. Section \ref{sec:methods} states the coincident-shock identification problem, the naive baseline, and the SPSC estimator. Section \ref{sec:data} describes the data. Section \ref{sec:results} reports the naive-versus-proximal contrast, the SPSC estimates and their identification diagnostics, and the robustness band. Section \ref{sec:discuss} discusses implications for public policy and crisis response.

# Background
\label{sec:bgresearch}

## Tourism in Hawaii

Hawaii's economy transitioned from a plantation-dominated model in the late 19th and early 20th centuries to tourism as the primary driver after statehood. The sugar and pineapple industries, controlled by a few powerful firms known as the "Big Five," peaked in the 1960s but declined due to global competition, labor costs, and diversification efforts. Statehood in 1959, combined with the introduction of jet air travel, spurred a tourism boom, with visitor numbers surging from 171,000 in 1958 to over 6.7 million by 1990 \citep{EconomicHistoryofHawaii}. This shift modernized the economy, increased population growth, and generated substantial revenue, but it also created dependency on external factors like air travel and international markets.

Tourism is central to Hawaii's fiscal health, generating $17.75 billion in visitor spending in 2019 alone, which supported $2.07 billion in state tax revenue and 216,000 jobs across direct, indirect, and induced sectors. On any given day in 2019, there were 249,000 visitors contributing $48.6 million in spending. Key islands like O'ahu (22.4 million daily spending) and Maui (14.0 million) bear the brunt of this activity \citep{HTA_2019}. Leisure and hospitality employment, a proxy for tourism-related jobs, hovered around 190,000-200,000 annually pre-2020, representing about one-third of the state's workforce. This reliance amplifies risks from shocks, as seen in past recessions, but also underscores tourism's role in funding public services and infrastructure.

Hawaii implemented some of the earliest and most aggressive COVID-19 containment policies in the United States. On March 4, 2020, Governor David Ige issued an emergency proclamation officially recognizing the virus as a statewide threat \citep[]{hawaii_emergency_2020}. Within weeks, the state began taking unprecedented measures alongside states like California \citep[]{pamscmcali}. On March 17, Governor Ige publicly urged all visitors to suspend their trips to Hawaii for 30 days, anticipating substantial economic damage to the state's tourism-dependent economy. \emph{"We do know there will be significant impact,"} he stated, though no concrete estimates were available at the time \citep[]{hawaii_tourism_suspension_2020}. A sweeping stay-at-home order followed on March 25, banning non-essential activities, closing non-critical businesses, and effectively shutting down day-to-day life and travel across the islands \citep[]{hawaii_stayhome_2020}. These actions were implemented alongside a mandatory 14-day quarantine on all arrivals, passed the same week, which further intensified the shutdown and isolated the state from both domestic and international travel. Despite the unprecedented scope of these interventions, no formal quantitative analysis has yet estimated the short-run economic effects of Hawaii's approach. This paper provides such an assessment.

## Literature Review
\label{sec:litrev}

The onset of the COVID-19 pandemic spurred a global wave of NPIs, with governments acting swiftly to limit viral transmission. Much of the early research focused on the public health rationale behind these policies—particularly the value of acting early to prevent exponential growth in cases. \citet{pamscmcali}, for instance, study California's shelter-in-place order and argue that its primary purpose was to delay the pandemic's peak, buying time for hospitals to prepare. They emphasize the importance of California's timing—implementing the policy while infection growth was still modest—as a key to its effectiveness.

Other studies reinforce the value of early, aggressive containment. Using SCM, \citet{yang2021does} analyzes Wuhan's lockdown and estimates substantial reductions in population movement and COVID-19 transmission, emphasizing the relevance of their findings for international public health policy. \citet{Cerqueti2021}, studying Italy's decision to close schools, stress that timing is critical when dealing with exponential contagion. They also note a political economy challenge: if containment is successful, the intervention may appear excessive in retrospect, raising political costs for early action. \citet{bayat2020syntheticcontrolsyntheticinterventions} offer a quantitative example, estimating that deaths in New York could have been reduced by over 80\% had lockdown been enacted ten days earlier. Outside of China and Europe, similar insights emerge. \citet{sobiech2022untimely} and \citet{li2023texas} document similar patterns in Brazil and Texas, finding that premature reopenings by state governments led to sustained spikes in cases.

Collectively, these studies underscore a key lesson: early interventions can mitigate public health disasters, but often at economic cost. This tradeoff between health and the economy became central to both policymaking and public discourse. \citet{osman2022economic} document how opponents of lockdowns, particularly in conservative circles, criticized them as economically inefficient and ineffective. \citet{gibson2023synthetic} evaluate statewide stay-at-home orders using synthetic control, focusing on new jobless claims as an economic indicator of interest. \citet{lee2022pandemic} examine the labor market impacts of COVID-19 in South Korea, highlighting the economic consequences of NPIs. \citet{hubeipda} study the economic impact of Hubei's lockdown. They show that while Hubei's lockdown caused a sharp downturn in the short term, the effects were short-lived—suggesting that delay or inaction might have led to more lasting harm.

Other work has assessed broader welfare outcomes of interventions. \citet{cole2020impact} show how the Wuhan lockdown reduced air pollution and associated mortality using augmented SCM. \citet{oliu2022effect} study vaccine mandates in Europe and estimate that increased vaccine uptake not only averted deaths but also prevented GDP losses—suggesting that public health policy can have broader economic upside when well-designed. Despite the breadth of this literature, Hawaii's case remains notably absent. Yet it represents perhaps the clearest U.S. example of an early, and most aggressive intervention. This paper contributes by bringing Hawaii into the empirical record and by offering credible estimates of the short-run economic costs of a ``zero-COVID'' style border \citep[]{yuan2022zero}.

While much has been learned about the effects of pandemic interventions, measuring their economic impacts remains challenging, and Hawaii pushes that challenge to an extreme. Most evaluations of anti-COVID policy rely on difference-in-differences (DiD) or synthetic control methods (SCM). Where cross-sectional variation in policy exists—some counties or states locking down while others do not—SCM and panel methods have been used productively \citep[e.g.,][]{yang2021does, hsiaoke2023, gong2024economic}. But these designs require unaffected or minimally affected units to serve as comparisons, and, as \citet{polevalpan} and \citet{covidturkey} note, that assumption collapses in a global pandemic where nearly every region was shocked at once. Every other U.S. state and comparable island economy faced its own pandemic disruption, so there is no untreated Hawaii to borrow from across space. To my knowledge the only study examining Hawaii's pandemic economy is \citet{bondsmith2022effects}, which provides valuable descriptive analysis but constructs no counterfactual.

One response to the missing-donor problem is to borrow strength across *time* rather than space. The Synthetic Historical Control (SHC) method of \citet{SHC} does exactly this, reconstructing the treated unit's counterfactual from its own pre-treatment trajectory. SHC is the natural naive baseline for Hawaii and I retain it as such. But borrowing across time does not, by itself, solve the deeper problem here. Whether the counterfactual is built from other states (classical SCM) or from Hawaii's own history (SHC), it is a world with *neither* the quarantine *nor* the pandemic; extrapolating it into 2020 and differencing against the observed series attributes the entire post-March collapse—pandemic and policy together—to the treatment. The issue is not the source of the donor information but the *coincidence* of two shocks in a single unit.

That is precisely the structure the *proximal* / *negative-control* literature was built to handle. Negative controls—variables driven by an unmeasured confounder but shielded from the treatment—have long been used to detect confounding \citep{lipsitch2010negative}; proximal causal inference turns them into an identification strategy, using proxies of a latent confounder to recover causal effects that ordinary adjustment cannot \citep{miao2018identifying,cui2024semiparametric,tchetgen2024introduction,shi2020selective}. \citet{parktchetgen2025} adapt this machinery to the synthetic-control setting as Single Proxy Synthetic Control, and \citet{synthsurr} develop a related surrogate-based proximal estimator. I apply SPSC to Hawaii because it is the one design in the synthetic-control family that concedes the pandemic confounder is present and unobservable and instruments it, rather than matching or conditioning it away.

# Methodology
\label{sec:methods}

We know what happened once Hawaii mandated two-week quarantines. We do not know what would have happened had it not. The difficulty, developed in Section~\ref{sec:idprob}, is that the event we want to switch off (the border policy) is perfectly aligned in time with an event we cannot switch off (the pandemic). Section~\ref{sec:naive} states the naive Synthetic Historical Control baseline and why it cannot separate the two. Section~\ref{sec:spsc} develops the Single Proxy Synthetic Control estimator that can, in principle, and Section~\ref{sec:altfail} explains why the other obvious candidates do not.

\textbf{Notation.} Let $\mathbb{R}$ denote the reals and $\|\cdot\|_1$ the usual $\ell_1$ norm. Sets are calligraphic ($\mathcal{T}, \mathcal{S}$), scalars lowercase ($h, t, n$), vectors bold lowercase, and matrices bold uppercase ($\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{Y}$). Let $\mathcal{T} = \{1, \dots, T\}$ index months. Treatment begins at $T_0+1$, with $\mathcal{T}_1 \defeq \{t \le T_0\}$ the pre-treatment period, $\mathcal{T}_2 \defeq \{t > T_0\}$ the post-treatment period, and $n = T - T_0$ the number of post periods. Let $d_t = \mathbf{1}\{t > T_0\}$ be the treatment indicator.

## The identification problem: a coincident common shock
\label{sec:idprob}

Following the Rubin potential-outcomes framework, let $y_t^1$ and $y_t^0$ be the treated and untreated potential outcomes for Hawaii at month $t$, with observed outcome $y_t = d_t y_t^1 + (1-d_t) y_t^0$. The object of interest is the average treatment effect on the treated over the post period,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:att}
\text{ATT} \defeq \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t \in \mathcal{T}_2}\left(y_t^1 - y_t^0\right),
\end{equation}
whose estimation requires a credible value for the unobserved $y_t^0$—what Hawaii's economy would have done after March 2020 had it *not* closed its border.

Suppose the untreated outcome follows a latent-factor model
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:factor}
y_t^0 = \mu_t + \boldsymbol{\beta}^\top \boldsymbol{\lambda}_t + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_t] = 0,
\end{equation}
where $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ collects time-varying latent factors and $\mu_t$ is a smooth secular component. In 2020 one coordinate of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ is the **pandemic**: a shock that is (i) unobserved, (ii) hits the outcome, and (iii) turns on at exactly the same month as the policy, so that $d_t$ and the pandemic factor are collinear over $\mathcal{T}_2$. Any estimator of $y_t^0$ that models Hawaii's untreated path as a continuation of its pre-2020 dynamics—whether across space or across time—sets the pandemic contribution $\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ to its *normal-times* value. Differencing the observed series against such a counterfactual then yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:contamination}
\widehat{y}_t^1 - \widehat{y}_t^0 = \underbrace{\big(y_t^1 - y_t^0\big)}_{\text{policy effect}} + \underbrace{\boldsymbol{\beta}^\top\big(\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t - \bar{\boldsymbol{\lambda}}\big)}_{\text{pandemic contamination}},
\end{equation}
the policy effect *plus* the pandemic's deviation from its normal path. The two are not separable from the treated unit alone, and, crucially, a good pre-treatment fit constrains only the first term's plausibility, not the second's size. This is the sense in which classical SC/DiD and SHC are all *naive* for this problem: they are unbiased for a treatment effect only if the pandemic factor is absent, which is exactly the case that does not hold.

## The naive baseline: Synthetic Historical Control
\label{sec:naive}

As the naive benchmark I use the Synthetic Historical Control (SHC) estimator of \citet{SHC}, the strongest member of the class that ignores the pandemic factor, since it needs no external donors at all.\footnote{Classical SCM estimates the counterfactual as $\mathbf{Y}_0 \mathbf{w}^\ast$ with $\mathbf{w}^\ast = \operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{w}\in\Delta^{N_0}} \|\mathbf{y}_1 - \mathbf{Y}_0\mathbf{w}\|_2^2$ over a simplex of unexposed donor units $\mathbf{Y}_0$. In a global pandemic no such unexposed $\mathbf{Y}_0$ exists, which is what motivates borrowing across time.} SHC reconstructs the treated unit's untreated path from overlapping windows of its *own* smoothed pre-treatment history. Concretely, it (i) smooths the pre-treatment series $\mathbf{y}_{\text{pre}}$ by local linear regression, (ii) forms a donor matrix $\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}}_{\text{pre}} \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times N}$ whose $N = T_0 - m - n + 1$ columns are contiguous length-$m$ segments of the smoothed series, (iii) matches the final length-$m$ evaluation window with simplex-constrained, ridge-regularized weights
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:shc_weights}
\mathbf{w}^\ast = \operatorname*{argmin}_{\mathbf{w} \ge \mathbf{0},\, \mathbf{1}^\top\mathbf{w}=1}\ \big\|\widetilde{\mathbf{y}}_{\text{eval}} - \widetilde{\mathbf{Y}}_{\text{pre}}\mathbf{w}\big\|_2^2 + \varsigma\,\big\|\mathbf{C}_0^\top\mathbf{w}\big\|_2^2,
\end{equation}
and (iv) applies those weights to the forward-shifted segments to extrapolate $\widehat{y}_t^0$ over $\mathcal{T}_2$. The number of historical segments is chosen by a forward-selection rule with a BIC-type early stop, and uncertainty is summarized by distribution-free conformal prediction intervals around the counterfactual. Because it borrows only from Hawaii's own smooth pre-2020 dynamics, the SHC counterfactual is a "business-as-usual 2020"—a world with neither the quarantine nor the pandemic—so its estimate carries the full contamination term in \eqref{eq:contamination}. It is exactly this over-attribution that the proximal design is meant to correct, and the size of the correction is the empirical payoff of Section~\ref{sec:results}.

## Single Proxy Synthetic Control
\label{sec:spsc}

The proximal strategy keeps the latent pandemic factor in the model and *instruments* it. A **negative control** (or proxy) is a variable that (i) is driven by the same latent confounder $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ as the outcome, but (ii) has **no causal path from the treatment**. It is the panel analogue of an instrument's exclusion restriction: it sees the pandemic, but it does not see the quarantine. Let $\mathbf{W}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{J}$ collect $J$ such controls—here the year-over-year growth of $J=5$ insulated employment sectors (Section~\ref{sec:data}). These fell in the pandemic recession (so they load on the macro coordinate of $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$) but do not depend on whether visitors can physically arrive in Hawaii (so no arrow runs from $d_t$ to $\mathbf{W}_t$).

SPSC \citep{parktchetgen2025} posits a linear **outcome bridge** $h^\star(\mathbf{W}_t) = \mathbf{W}_t^\top \boldsymbol{\gamma}^\star$ that reconstructs the treated unit's untreated outcome in conditional mean:
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:bridge}
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,y_t^0 - \mathbf{W}_t^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\star \,\middle|\, \boldsymbol{\lambda}_t\right] = 0 \qquad \text{for } t \in \mathcal{T}_1.
\end{equation}
Because $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ is unobserved, \eqref{eq:bridge} cannot be fit by ordinary least squares. SPSC's key move for a single treated unit is to use the treated series' **own pre-period history as the instrument**: under a relevance condition (below), the treated unit's pre-treatment information is correlated with $\boldsymbol{\lambda}_t$ but, in the pre-period, orthogonal to the bridge residual, giving the moment condition
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:gmm}
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\,\mathbf{Z}_t\left(y_t - \mathbf{W}_t^\top\boldsymbol{\gamma}\right)\right] = \mathbf{0}, \qquad t \in \mathcal{T}_1,
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{Z}_t$ is built from the treated unit's pre-period information. The bridge coefficients $\boldsymbol{\gamma}^\star$ are estimated by **ridge-regularized GMM** on \eqref{eq:gmm}, the ridge penalty stabilizing the solution when the controls are collinear. Optionally the treated and control series are first **de-trended** against a B-spline basis (the SPSC-DT variant used throughout), removing smooth secular drift $\mu_t$ so that the bridge is fit on the factor-driven variation identification actually rests on. The counterfactual and effect path are then
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spsc_cf}
\widehat{y}_t^0 = \mathbf{W}_t^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}, \qquad \widehat{\alpha}_t = y_t - \widehat{y}_t^0 \ \ (t \in \mathcal{T}_2), \qquad \widehat{\text{ATT}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}_2}\widehat{\alpha}_t,
\end{equation}
with a GMM sandwich standard error for $\widehat{\text{ATT}}$ and, as a finite-sample cross-check, a distribution-free conformal prediction band. The full mechanics—assumptions, the ridge-GMM estimator, and the conformal construction—are given in \citet{parktchetgen2025} and the \texttt{mlsynth} documentation.

\textbf{The relevance diagnostic.} SPSC's identifying relevance condition (its Assumption~3, the analogue of a strong first stage) requires the controls to genuinely comove with the treated series in the pre-period. Its empirical symptom of *weak* relevance is a pre-period fit no better than the treated series' own scale: a pre-treatment root-mean-squared error comparable to the treated series' standard deviation. I therefore report, for every outcome, the ratio
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:rmsesd}
\rho \defeq \frac{\text{RMSE}_{\text{pre}}}{\text{SD}(\mathbf{y}_{\text{pre}})}
\end{equation}
as the identification gauge. Values well below 1 indicate a usable synthetic control; $\rho \to 1$ means the donors barely track the treated unit and the estimate should be read as a **bound**, not a point. I label outcomes *well-identified* ($\rho < 0.85$), *borderline* ($0.85 \le \rho < 0.98$), or *weakly identified* ($\rho \ge 0.98$).

\textbf{What the insulated sectors can and cannot span.} The pandemic is not one factor but (at least) two: a **macro-recession factor**—the general contraction, spanned by the insulated employment sectors—and a **travel-demand-collapse factor**—people ceasing to fly anywhere out of fear, independent of any Hawaii policy. The insulated sectors span the first but not the second. SPSC built on them alone therefore reconstructs only the macro component of the counterfactual and cannot subtract the travel-demand collapse. Consequently its tourism ATT **over-attributes** the drop to the policy: it is an **upper bound in magnitude** on the border-closure effect, with the *observed* collapse equal to policy plus travel-demand loss. Closing the gap would require an external travel-demand negative control—inbound passengers to a comparable destination that was exposed to the pandemic but did not lock down (e.g., Florida)—which is left to future work (Section~\ref{sec:discuss}). This is why the tourism results below are reported as a band and framed as bounds, while the broad activity index, which rides the macro factor the insulated sectors *do* span, is the one series I read as a point.

## Why the alternatives fail
\label{sec:altfail}

Several tempting designs were considered and rejected; each breaks on the coincident-shock structure of Section~\ref{sec:idprob}. **Classical synthetic control** matches the pandemic into the counterfactual and so confounds policy with pandemic. **Synthetic instrumental variables** need an instrument that shifts treatment but not the outcome directly; the treatment here is a single deterministic policy switch coincident with the shock, and no such instrument exists. **Forecast-based structural-break tests** cannot distinguish a latent level shift that is coincident with treatment from the treatment effect itself, and would assign the whole shift to the policy. **Surrogate methods** \citep{synthsurr} require a separable effect/confounder channel and post-treatment surrogates predictive of the effect; here the confounder and the effect arrive together and no clean surrogate is available. **Orthogonalized synthetic control** sharpens *inference* under a maintained identification but does not solve the *identification* of a confounder coincident with treatment—it operates at the wrong layer. Proximal / negative-control inference is almost uniquely suited to this problem because it is the one framework that concedes the confounder is present and unobservable and instruments it.

# Data
\label{sec:data}

I assemble a monthly panel for Hawaii spanning January 1991 to December 2020, joining two public sources on month. All series are expressed as annualized year-over-year (YoY) growth rates. This transformation mitigates nonstationary trends and lets treatment effects be read directly as percentage-point changes in growth.

The **treated outcomes** are ten tourism and labor series from Hawaii's Department of Business, Economic Development \& Tourism (DBEDT) and the Federal Reserve Economic Data (FRED) system: `Visitor Arrivals`, `Visitor Days`, `Occupancy`, `Mean Daily Rate`, `Revenue per Available Room`, `Accommodation Emp`, `Total Leisure Emp`, `Unemp Rate`, `LFP`, and the Coincident `Econ Activity Index`. Every one of these is *downstream of the border closure*: it moves when the ability of visitors to arrive changes, so it can only ever be a treated series, never a control.

The **negative-control donors** are five *insulated* employment sectors from the DBEDT Monthly Economic Indicators, in YoY growth: `NatRes_Constr_Emp`, `Wholesale_Emp`, `Financial_Emp`, `HealthCare_Emp`, and `Government_Emp`. These industries were hit by the pandemic's macro-recession shock—falling roughly 7--12\% in the 2020 trough—but do not depend on whether tourists can physically enter Hawaii, so no causal path runs from the quarantine to them. They are the empirical negative controls of Section~\ref{sec:spsc}. @fig-premise contrasts the two groups: the treated tourism series collapse by 50--99\% at the border closure while the insulated donors dip only modestly, the visual signature of a factor structure in which the donors carry the macro shock and the tourism series carry the macro shock *plus* the travel-demand collapse *plus* the policy.

The treatment indicator `Mandatory Quarantine` switches to 1 in March 2020, giving 10 post-treatment months (March--December 2020). Although the panel ships the full 1991--2020 history, the analysis truncates the pre-period to a recent window beginning **January 2014** (74 pre-treatment months). Three decades of stale comovement is less relevant to the 2020 counterfactual than the recent history, and the 2014 window empirically sharpens the relevance ratios of \eqref{eq:rmsesd} and yields non-degenerate GMM standard errors that the full-history-plus-detrend combination did not. The full-panel version is available by removing the truncation and enters the robustness band of Section~\ref{sec:results}.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
#| label: setup-analysis

import warnings; warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.dates as mdates
from mlsynth import SHC, PROXIMAL

DATA = "Data/hawaii_proximal_panel.csv"
START, TREAT = "2014-01-01", "Mandatory Quarantine"
DONORS = ["NatRes_Constr_Emp", "Wholesale_Emp", "Financial_Emp",
          "HealthCare_Emp", "Government_Emp"]
DLAB = {"NatRes_Constr_Emp": "Nat. Res. & Constr.", "Wholesale_Emp": "Wholesale Trade",
        "Financial_Emp": "Financial Activities", "HealthCare_Emp": "Health Care",
        "Government_Emp": "Government"}
TOURISM = ["Visitor Arrivals", "Visitor Days", "Occupancy", "Mean Daily Rate",
           "Revenue per Available Room", "Accommodation Emp"]
ECON = ["Total Leisure Emp", "Unemp Rate", "LFP", "Econ Activity Index"]
ALL_OUT = TOURISM + ECON

_full = pd.read_csv(DATA, parse_dates=["Date"])
wide = _full[_full["Date"] >= pd.Timestamp(START)].reset_index(drop=True)

def _long(w, oc, donors=DONORS):
    fr = []
    t = w[["Date", oc, TREAT]].rename(columns={oc: "y", TREAT: "treat"})
    t["unit"] = oc; t["treat"] = t["treat"].astype(int)
    fr.append(t[["unit", "Date", "y", "treat"]])
    for d in donors:
        f = w[["Date", d]].rename(columns={d: "y"}); f["unit"] = d; f["treat"] = 0
        fr.append(f[["unit", "Date", "y", "treat"]])
    return pd.concat(fr, ignore_index=True).rename(columns={"Date": "time"})

def spsc_fit(w, oc, donors=DONORS, detrend=True, conformal=False,
             spline_df=None, basis_degree=None, display=False):
    """Fit SPSC-DT. display=True renders mlsynth's native two-panel graph."""
    long = _long(w, oc, donors)
    cfg = {"df": long, "outcome": "y", "treat": "treat", "unitid": "unit",
           "time": "time", "methods": ["SPSC"], "donors": donors,
           "spsc_detrend": detrend, "spsc_conformal": conformal,
           "display_graphs": display, "save": False}
    if spline_df is not None: cfg["spsc_spline_df"] = spline_df
    if basis_degree is not None: cfg["spsc_basis_degree"] = basis_degree
    res = PROXIMAL(cfg).fit()
    tr = long[long.unit == oc].sort_values("time")
    y = tr["y"].to_numpy(float)
    t0 = int((tr["treat"].to_numpy() == 0).sum())
    cf = np.asarray(res.counterfactual, float).ravel()
    rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y[:t0] - cf[:t0]) ** 2)))
    sd = float(np.std(y[:t0]))
    rho = rmse / sd if sd else float("nan")
    ident = ("well-identified" if rho < 0.85
             else "borderline" if rho < 0.98 else "weakly identified (bound)")
    se = float(res.att_se) if res.att_se is not None else float("nan")
    return {"att": float(res.att), "se": se, "rho": rho, "ident": ident}

def shc_fit(w, oc, display=False):
    """Fit the naive Synthetic Historical Control baseline (own history)."""
    sub = w[["Date", oc, TREAT]].copy(); sub["Unit"] = "Hawaii"
    r = SHC({"df": sub, "outcome": oc, "treat": TREAT, "unitid": "Unit",
             "time": "Date", "m": 12 * 5, "display_graphs": display,
             "save": False}).fit()
    return float(r.effects.att)

def md_table(df):
    cols = list(df.columns)
    rows = ["| " + " | ".join(map(str, cols)) + " |",
            "|" + "|".join([" --- "] * len(cols)) + "|"]
    for _, r in df.iterrows():
        rows.append("| " + " | ".join(str(v) for v in r) + " |")
    return "\n".join(rows)

def _pp(x):
    return f"{abs(x):.0f}"

# Diagnostics across all outcomes (numeric; no per-call graphs)
_diag = []
for oc in ALL_OUT:
    f = spsc_fit(wide, oc)
    _diag.append([oc, "tourism" if oc in TOURISM else "econ/labor",
                  f"{f['att']:.1f}", f"{f['se']:.1f}", f"{f['rho']:.2f}", f["ident"]])
diag_df = pd.DataFrame(_diag, columns=["Outcome", "Group", "ATT",
                                       "GMM SE", "RMSE/SD ($\\rho$)", "Identification"])

# Naive-vs-proximal contrast for the headline outcomes
_HEAD = ["Visitor Days", "Occupancy", "Revenue per Available Room",
         "Accommodation Emp", "Econ Activity Index"]
_con, _shc, _spsc = [], {}, {}
for oc in _HEAD:
    _shc[oc] = shc_fit(wide, oc); _spsc[oc] = spsc_fit(wide, oc)["att"]
    _con.append([oc, f"{_shc[oc]:.1f}", f"{_spsc[oc]:.1f}", f"{_shc[oc]-_spsc[oc]:.1f}"])
con_df = pd.DataFrame(_con, columns=["Outcome", "Naive SHC", "Proximal SPSC",
                                     "Gap (pandemic)"])

# Specification robustness band
_BAND = ["Visitor Days", "Occupancy", "Revenue per Available Room", "Econ Activity Index"]
_band = {}
for oc in _BAND:
    a = np.array([
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, detrend=True)["att"],
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, detrend=False)["att"],
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, basis_degree=2)["att"],
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, spline_df=6)["att"],
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, donors=[d for d in DONORS if d != "Government_Emp"])["att"],
        spsc_fit(wide, oc, donors=[d for d in DONORS if d != "HealthCare_Emp"])["att"],
        spsc_fit(_full, oc, detrend=True)["att"],
    ])
    _band[oc] = a
band_df = pd.DataFrame(
    [[oc, f"{_band[oc].min():.1f}", f"{np.median(_band[oc]):.1f}", f"{_band[oc].max():.1f}"]
     for oc in _BAND],
    columns=["Outcome", "Min", "Median", "Max"])

# Scalars quoted in prose
vd_shc, vd_spsc = _shc["Visitor Days"], _spsc["Visitor Days"]
vd_gap = vd_shc - vd_spsc
eai_shc, eai_spsc = _shc["Econ Activity Index"], _spsc["Econ Activity Index"]
eai_gap = eai_shc - eai_spsc
eai_rho = spsc_fit(wide, "Econ Activity Index")["rho"]
vd_rho = spsc_fit(wide, "Visitor Days")["rho"]
vd_band = _band["Visitor Days"]
```

Right: the five insulated-sector donors dip only modestly---they carry the pandemic's macro-recession factor but not the travel-demand collapse or the policy. The dotted line marks March 2020."

```{python}
    a1.plot(wide["Date"], wide[oc], lw=1.2, label=oc, color=c)
for d in DONORS:

for ax, ti in ((a1, "Treated tourism outcomes"), (a2, "Insulated-sector donors")):
```

\section{Results}
\label{sec:results}

## The naive-versus-proximal contrast

The central methodological point is visible in a single comparison: the same treated series, estimated first with the naive Synthetic Historical Control baseline and then with proximal SPSC. @fig-shc-vd and @fig-spsc-vd show it for Visitor Days. The naive SHC counterfactual (@fig-shc-vd) is a business-as-usual 2020 built from Hawaii's own smooth pre-pandemic history; differencing against it attributes essentially the entire post-March collapse to the policy, giving an ATT of `{python} f"{vd_shc:.1f}"` percentage points. The SPSC counterfactual (@fig-spsc-vd) instead reconstructs Hawaii's untreated path from the insulated sectors, which *net out the pandemic's macro-recession component*, and returns a smaller ATT of `{python} f"{vd_spsc:.1f}"` points.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-shc-vd
#| fig-cap: "Naive baseline (Synthetic Historical Control), Visitor Days. The counterfactual is built from Hawaii's own pre-2020 history, so it is a world with neither the pandemic nor the policy and the full collapse loads onto the estimate."
_ = shc_fit(wide, "Visitor Days", display=True)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-spsc-vd
#| fig-cap: "Proximal Single Proxy Synthetic Control, Visitor Days. The counterfactual (left panel) is reconstructed from the insulated-sector negative controls, netting out the pandemic's macro-recession factor; the gap panel (right) is the estimated effect path."
_ = spsc_fit(wide, "Visitor Days", conformal=True, display=True)
```

The `{python} _pp(vd_gap)`-point gap between the two estimates is not noise: it is the pandemic's macro-recession contribution from \eqref{eq:contamination}, which the naive design silently charges to the border policy and which SPSC removes by instrumenting it. The same wedge appears across the headline outcomes (@tbl-contrast). It is largest, in level terms, for the broad Economic Activity Index, where the naive ATT of `{python} f"{eai_shc:.1f}"` points shrinks to `{python} f"{eai_spsc:.1f}"` under SPSC---a `{python} _pp(eai_gap)`-point pandemic component---because that index is precisely the series most exposed to the general recession the insulated sectors span.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(md_table(con_df))
print("\n: Naive SHC versus proximal SPSC average treatment effects "
      "(percentage points of year-over-year growth), headline outcomes. The "
      "gap is the pandemic's macro-recession component the naive design cannot "
      "net out. {#tbl-contrast}\n")
```

@fig-shc-eai and @fig-spsc-eai repeat the contrast for the Economic Activity Index; here the SPSC pre-treatment gap (the right-hand panel) hugs zero tightly, foreshadowing the identification diagnostics below.

```{python}

#| label: fig-shc-eai

_ = shc_fit(wide, "Econ Activity Index", display=True)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

_ = spsc_fit(wide, "Econ Activity Index", conformal=True, display=True)
```

## SPSC estimates and the identification gauge

@tbl-diag reports SPSC-DT across all ten outcomes together with the relevance ratio $\rho$ of \eqref{eq:rmsesd} and its identification label. Reading the table requires the discipline the ratio was introduced for: a point estimate is only as trustworthy as its pre-period fit.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(md_table(diag_df))
print("\n: SPSC-DT estimates and identification diagnostics, all outcomes. "
      "ATT is in percentage points of year-over-year growth; the GMM SE is the "
      "sandwich standard error; $\\rho$ is the pre-period RMSE/SD relevance "
      "gauge. {#tbl-diag}\n")
```

Three readings follow. First, **the tourism-demand collapse is large and robust**: Visitor Days, Visitor Arrivals, Occupancy, and Revenue per Available Room all show a $\sim$65--75-point year-over-year drop against the proximal counterfactual, and a pre-period RMSE of only a couple of points against a $\sim$70-point effect is a strong signal-to-effect ratio. Second, **the relevance ratios still sit near 1 for most tourism series** ($\rho \approx$ `{python} f"{vd_rho:.2f}"` for Visitor Days), because the insulated sectors under-span the tourism factor (Section~\ref{sec:spsc}); Occupancy and Revenue per Available Room are the best tourism cases ($\rho \approx 0.89$, borderline). These tourism ATTs are therefore best read as **upper bounds in magnitude** on the *policy* effect, with the observed drop equal to policy plus the travel-demand collapse. Third, **the one cleanly identified series is the Economic Activity Index** ($\rho =$ `{python} f"{eai_rho:.2f}"`, well-identified): riding the macro-recession factor the insulated sectors span, SPSC reconstructs its counterfactual well, and its $\sim$12-point drop is the single most trustworthy number in the table.

Two caveats attach to the GMM standard errors. On this 2014 window they are non-degenerate and usable for the visitor and activity series ($\sim$3--8 points), a genuine improvement over the full-history window where de-trending a near-interpolating fit collapses the sandwich toward zero. But two of the labor series remain unreliable---the Unemployment Rate ATT is a relative-growth artifact with a near-zero SE, and the Labor Force Participation SE is tiny---and should not be read at face value. More fundamentally, even a well-behaved SE captures only *sampling* noise around the pre-period bridge, not the *extrapolation* risk of transporting that bridge across the March-2020 structural break, which is the dominant uncertainty here. I therefore do not lean on the SE alone.

## Robustness: a specification band, not a point

Because the honest uncertainty is extrapolation risk rather than sampling noise, I report the headline effects as a **band** built from specification sensitivity: de-trending on versus off, the B-spline degrees of freedom, the polynomial basis degree, dropping each of the two largest-weight donors, and the full-1991 versus 2014 window. @tbl-band collects the minimum, median, and maximum SPSC ATT across these specifications for the four best-behaved outcomes.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
print(md_table(band_df))
print("\n: Specification robustness band. Minimum, median, and maximum SPSC "
      "ATT (percentage points) across seven specifications: de-trend on/off, "
      "spline df, basis degree, two donor-subset drops, and the 2014 versus "
      "full-1991 window. {#tbl-band}\n")
```

For the visitor-volume series the band runs roughly from `{python} f"{vd_band.min():.0f}"` to `{python} f"{vd_band.max():.0f}"` points (median `{python} f"{np.median(vd_band):.0f}"`), so the defensible statement is a $\sim$60--75-point *upper-bound* collapse in tourism demand rather than any single figure. The Economic Activity Index band is both narrower and shallower, consistent with its being the cleanly identified case. Taken together, the diagnostics and the band say the same thing: the border closure sits on top of a large tourism-demand collapse that the insulated sectors cannot fully separate from it, so the tourism numbers bound the policy effect from above while the broad activity index gives the one point estimate the data can support.

# Discussion
\label{sec:discuss}

The methodological lesson of Hawaii is that a good pre-treatment fit is not identification when a policy and a global shock arrive in the same month. A naive synthetic control—whether it borrows across states or, as in SHC, across the treated unit's own history—produces a clean-looking counterfactual and a large ATT, but that ATT is the border-closure effect plus the pandemic's contribution to Hawaii's outcomes, and nothing in the fit reveals the mix. Proximal / negative-control inference is the discipline that separates them: by instrumenting the latent pandemic factor with insulated employment sectors that carry it but are immune to the policy, SPSC nets out the macro-recession component the naive design cannot. The wedge between the two estimates—about `{python} _pp(vd_gap)` points for Visitor Days and `{python} _pp(eai_gap)` points for the activity index—is a direct, quantitative measure of how much pandemic contamination a naive reading would have mistaken for policy.

At the same time, the analysis is candid about the limit of what the shipped data can identify. The insulated sectors span the pandemic's general-recession factor but not its travel-demand-collapse factor: even with an open border, Hawaii tourism would have fallen sharply as people stopped flying. SPSC on insulated sectors alone therefore recovers only the macro component of the counterfactual, and the resulting tourism ATTs over-attribute the collapse to the policy—they are upper bounds in magnitude, which is why I report them as a band. The single cleanly identified effect is the broad Economic Activity Index, whose $\sim$12-point drop rides the macro factor the donors do span. The substantive conclusion is thus deliberately modest and, I would argue, more credible for it: the border closure coincided with a near-total collapse in measured tourism demand, of which a bounded share is causally the policy, and it accompanied a well-identified $\sim$12-point contraction in broad economic activity.

The decisive next step is to close the two-factor gap with an external travel-demand negative control: inbound passengers to a comparable destination that was exposed to the pandemic but did **not** lock down, with Florida the leading candidate. Such a donor would carry the travel-demand-collapse factor the insulated sectors miss, and adding it should tighten the tourism ATTs toward the policy-only effect—a smaller magnitude than the insulated-only bound. Two cautions from the present work carry forward: a no-lockdown donor tends to be *under*-weighted because its pre-2020 comovement with Hawaii tourism is weak, so simply adding it need not fix identification on its own; and near-collinear open destinations added *en masse* induce large offsetting weights and hurt the fit. Puerto Rico, tempting as a fellow island, is not a valid control—it imposed its own stay-at-home order in mid-March 2020 and is a contaminated, treated-like unit that, if anything, bounds the effect from the other side.

These estimates speak only to short-run economic outcomes through the end of 2020 and do not weigh the public-health benefits—lives saved, hospital strain averted—against the economic cost. What the paper does provide is a credibly bounded price tag for decisive early action, and a template for evaluating it: when the intervention and the crisis it responds to are one and the same event in time, the analyst's task is not to find a cleaner comparison unit but to find a variable that sees the crisis and not the policy.

# Conclusion

This paper estimates the short-run economic consequences of Hawaii's March 2020 mandatory quarantine while confronting the identification problem that its predecessors on this topic could not: for a single treated unit, the border-closure policy and the COVID-19 pandemic are perfectly collinear in time, so no synthetic control that merely matches Hawaii to a pre-pandemic counterfactual can separate the two. I resolve this with Single Proxy Synthetic Control, a proximal / negative-control estimator that instruments the latent pandemic factor using insulated employment sectors that carry the pandemic's macro-recession shock but are immune to the border policy.

Contrasting SPSC with a naive Synthetic Historical Control baseline shows that a substantial share of the measured tourism collapse—roughly `{python} _pp(vd_gap)` percentage points for Visitor Days—is pandemic contamination the naive design charges to the policy. SPSC recovers a large, robust tourism-demand collapse (about 60--75 points of year-over-year growth for the visitor-volume series) but, because the insulated sectors span only the macro-recession factor, identifies it weakly-to-borderline; these tourism effects are upper bounds in magnitude on the policy effect and are reported as a robustness band rather than as points. The one cleanly identified series is the Coincident Economic Activity Index ($\rho =$ `{python} f"{eai_rho:.2f}"`), whose $\sim$12-point contraction is the most trustworthy single estimate.

Methodologically, the study demonstrates how negative-control inference disciplines causal claims when a policy and a global shock coincide—a structure common to pandemic border closures, but also to climate shocks and other systemic crises where a would-be counterfactual unit is itself engulfed by the event. Substantively, it delivers a bounded, honest estimate of the economic price of Hawaii's ``Great Isolation with Aloha characteristics'', and points to a concrete path—an external no-lockdown travel-demand donor—for sharpening that bound into a point.
